newsitem.title: USA: U.S. beefs up forces in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: U.S. beefs up forces in Gulf.

text.p: President Bill Clinton accelerated the buildup of U.S. forces in the Gulf despite a pledge by Iraq that it will stop attacking U.S. warplanes patrolling an expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq.

Clinton on Friday ordered 5,000 additional infantry troops to Kuwait to join 1,200 soldiers already holding exercises near the Iraqi border and dispatched Defence Secretary William Perry to the Gulf to discuss potential military moves.

Washington welcomed Iraq's latest pronouncements aimed at defusing two weeks of tension with the United States, but said it would not rule out a further missile attack on Iraq as long as U.S. pilots were in danger.
A spokesman for Iraq's ruling Revolutionary Command Council on Friday said attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes patrolling no-fly zones would stop as of midnight local time (2000 GMT).
But U.S. officials said they were waiting for Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to honour those promises.

"They're welcome words, but our main concern here is the safety of the pilots and that depends not on his words, but his actions," National Security Adviser Anthony Lake told ABC-TV's "Nightline programme.
"We'll have to see what he does on the ground," Lake said. "We will do what is necessary to protect our pilots."

Clinton met his top national security advisers at the White House late on Friday for 90 minutes to decide the next moves in the showdown with Iraq, including Perry's trip to the region, with scheduled stops in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

Perry, also likely to visit Turkey and Bahrain, will be trying to shore up support among U.S. allies, while at home, other advisers like Lake will be trying to ensure congressional support for any military action that is decided.
"I think that the reports of the demise of the coalition are entirely premature," Lake said, rejecting reports that Britain and France have been tepid in their support.

With further military strikes being considered virtually inevitable around Washington, White House officials said Clinton would not be rushed and was taking time to build support among reluctant allies and the American public.

"He wants to build a consensus. It's important," one official said in noting that the president was willing to defer an immediate strike briefly to strengthen its diplomatic and political underpinnings, especially this close to the Nov. 5 U.S. presidential election.
Lake admitted that the administration needed to improve its consultations with Congress and said efforts were under way to rectify the situation in coming days.

Earlier, the Pentagon said the 5,000 soldiers based at Fort Hood, Texas, would depart this weekend for Kuwait as part of a military buildup in the Gulf, that includes beefing up planes and warships in the region.

Eight sleek, radar-dodging Stealth warplanes have already arrived in Kuwait and a second U.S. aircraft carrier, the Enterprise, is steaming toward the Gulf, which will bring the force there to over 150 Navy aircraft and over 20 other warships and submarines, many armed with cruise missiles.
Lake said he was confident the United States could prevent another Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, the action that prompted the 1991 Gulf War.
"I think we can deter him, and if he were to invade Kuwait, defeat him," Lake told ABC.

Washington has faced criticism for pulling back from Kurdish-controlled northern Iraq after one Kurdish group enlisted the aid of Iraqi forces to wrest control from a rival faction. "There has been a shift in circumstance," not policy, Lake said, stressing the U.S. commitment to help the Kurds.
Eleven U.S. refugee-assistance groups Friday urged Washington to provide a "safe haven" for up to 1,000 Kurdish citizens who have worked for U.S. humanitarian agencies there.

In a joint letter to the State Department, the groups said they had information that some Kurdish citizens working for such U.S. groups were "captured and summarily executed" by forces back by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Lake said the United States viewed the south of Iraq as its primary area of strategic interest, but would do "everything practical to try to manifest our support for the Kurdish people" in the north.
